description: We are six Information Systems students at the Federal University of Uberlândia (UFU) in Brazil: Celina Vieira, Gabriel Esquivel, Isabela Dantas, Isabela Rocha, Leandro Elias, and Leandro Pina. Outside of class, we spend most of our time building AI projects, doing academic research, competing in programming contests, and making 3D games. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are taking on Flame in Freefall to make microgravity combustion data easier to explore and interact with.
summary:
AstroFire 3D is an interactive fire safety console, 3D Unity WebGL simulator, and Super Intelligence (SI) copilot built on open NASA space combustion data.

On Earth, hot air rises and gives fire a teardrop shape, but in space flames form quiet blue spheres that behave very differently. Standard ground tests miss these risks, and NASA’s data is scattered across technical databases (PSI and NTRS). To solve this, we built a physics engine grounded on 79 verified BASS-II tests from the ISS (R² = 0.91 for flame-spread prediction). We then added 71 more ISS flight states to train a physics-informed neural network that predicts whether a flame survives, reaching 95.3% cross-validated accuracy and catching 97.7% of sustained fires. We also rank six NASA campaigns (BASS-II, Saffire, SoFIE, SAME, FLEX and SPICE) by relevance to four space habitats.

Users test 7 real NASA materials across the ISS (0g), Moon (0.16g), Mars (0.38g), and Earth (1g), adjusting oxygen and airflow to see burn speed, minimum oxygen limit, CO and CO₂ gases, live 3D flame behavior, and generate an analysis report. As an extra feature, we integrated microgravity heat transfer research from Brazil, our homeland, to size water-mist extinguisher suppression. Every result separates direct NASA data from estimates, supporting safer space missions and fire safety on Earth.

Make the next giant leap safer!
details:
AstroFire 3D is an interactive 3D microgravity combustion simulator, physics-informed AI platform, and fire-safety engineering console built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Flame in Freefall). Its purpose is to transform empirical records from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) into an accessible, real-time decision tool for spacecraft cabins and partial-gravity habitats.

Fire in space behaves nothing like fire on Earth. Without buoyancy-driven convection, hot gases do not rise: flames in quiescent microgravity (0g) form slow, faint blue spherical diffusion balls, yet even a gentle cabin ventilation breeze (4–10 cm/s) or partial gravity (Moon at 0.16g, Mars at 0.38g) can feed fresh oxygen into the reaction zone and cause a flame to spread faster or ignite at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth. AstroFire 3D bridges this gap by combining a deterministic physics engine, a custom Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), real-time 3D Unity WebGL combustion animations, and an operational fire-extinguisher sizing calculator within a single unified web console.

Project & Repository Access

Live Application (3D Simulator & Console): https://astrofire-3d.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository (Backend, PINN, Frontend, 3D Unity & Contracts): https://github.com/leandro-elias-fontes/AstroFire-3D-hackathon

The Problem

Over decades of orbital research, NASA has conducted high-precision combustion experiments inside spacecraft gloveboxes and Orbital Test Beds—such as BASS-II, Saffire I–VI, SoFIE, FLEX, and SAME. Because every burn in microgravity requires astronaut crew time and launch mass, the resulting datasets are fragmented across heterogeneous tables, technical reports, and PDFs, often with small sample sizes (e.g., 79 verified state transitions in BASS-II).

For engineers, researchers, and students, interpreting how a given material behaves across different gravity regimes (0g ISS, 0.16g Moon, 0.38g Mars, 1.0g Earth), oxygen concentrations, and cabin airflows requires cross-referencing multiple reports and analytical equations. Furthermore, numbers in a spreadsheet alone do not convey the operational danger of a nearly invisible blue 0g flame—nor do they answer the immediate crew-safety question: if a fire starts under these conditions, how much water mist and how much time will it take to extinguish it?

The Gap

Advances in AI and browser-based 3D simulation create new opportunities to explore aerospace fire-safety archives, but generic LLM wrappers or black-box neural networks are not suitable for spacecraft safety:

  1. Hallucination and Offline Risk: Wrapping an external LLM API can fabricate physical numbers, violate conservation laws, or fail when offline during judging or mission operations.
  2. Small-N Overfitting: A conventional black-box neural network trained on 79 experimental rows easily overfits and violates thermodynamics—such as predicting sustained fire below a material's Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI).
  3. Lack of Operational Suppression Sizing & Partial-Gravity Data: NASA's PSI archive contains no solid-material combustion tests conducted in partial gravity (0.16g Moon or 0.38g Mars), and existing tools rarely translate combustion physics into actionable fire-extinguisher requirements (water volume and discharge time) tailored to reduced-gravity boiling physics.

Our Solution

AstroFire 3D solves these challenges with a zero-dependency, sub-5ms deterministic Python backend (FastAPI + Pydantic V2) paired with our own custom Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), a real-time Unity WebGL 3D combustion chamber, and a Suppression Sizing Module that integrates NASA data with Brazilian microgravity thermal research.

Every simulation explicitly declares its scientific boundary:

  • Empirical Match (empirical_bass2): Directly retrieves verified ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox measurements from BASS-II (PSI-25, DOI: 10.60555/4qc4-de67, CC0-1.0) across 7 spacecraft materials (PMMA clear slabs, thin films, clear/black rods, SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric, Nomex III fire barrier, and Japan wax candles). We also audited dataset licenses, strictly excluding PSI-10 due to its lack of an open license.
  • Physics-Bounded Interpolation (interpolated_from_ntrs): When testing custom environmental combinations or partial gravity, the engine computes Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI), flame spread rate (Vf), and toxic gas byproducts (CO ppm and CO2 %) using analytical equations from NASA/TM-20210011385, Saffire I–VI, SoFIE, FLEX, and SAME.

Our Core Differentiators

1. Custom Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) with High Accuracy

Instead of relying on external AI APIs or black-box models, we engineered our own Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) and Physics-Informed Classifier from scratch in pure Python math (backend/app/ml_pipeline.py). We embedded the governing physical laws from NASA/TM-20210011385 directly into the feature space and loss function alongside 24 physics collocation boundary points:

  • Olson Eq. (6.1): U-shaped microgravity Limiting Oxygen Index boundary (XO2(a) = 6e^-0.5a + 0.0167a + LOImin).
  • Bhattacharjee Eq. (2.2)–(2.5): Thermally thin/thick inverse thickness scaling (Vf ∝ τ^-α) and radiative quench velocity (Vg,cr).
  • T'ien Concurrent/Opposed Flow Limits: High-velocity Damköhler blow-off boundaries.

Validated with Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation on the 79 ISS empirical states (running full training in ~650 ms on CPU), our custom network achieved:

  • 94.94% Classification Accuracy, 95.31% Precision, 98.39% Recall, and 96.83% F1-Score in distinguishing sustained flame spread from radiative quench/extinction.
  • R² = 0.9117, RMSE = 0.1747 mm/s, and MAE = 0.0549 mm/s in predicting microgravity flame spread rates (Vf).
2. Real-Time 3D Microgravity Chamber & Original Voxel Animation

To make invisible 0g combustion intuitive, we built an interactive 3D combustion chamber in Unity (WebGL) paired with original 3D voxel models (Earth, ISS, Moon, Mars, RocketShip, and Fire Extinguisher) sculpted by our team in MagicaVoxel. The 3D animation is driven in real time by four physical outputs from our backend (flame_geometry, burn_rate_mm_s, flame_color_hex, and oxygen_factor). In quiescent 0g, the custom particle shader renders a spherical #3B82F6 blue diffusion flame; as airflow or gravity increases, it stretches into an elongated, soot-radiating #F97316 orange plume, and smoothly quenches into dissipating smoke over 600 ms whenever oxygen drops below the material's LOI.

3. Beyond NASA Data: Brazilian Microgravity Research (UFSC/INPE) & Fire Extinguisher Sizing

To answer how much water and time are required to put out a fire in space, we went beyond NASA's datasets and incorporated Brazilian microgravity thermal research conducted by the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC) and the National Institute for Space Research (INPE) aboard the VSB-30 sounding rocket, combining it with NASA's Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (FWM PFE) qualification data (NTRS-20130011664, 2,720 mL tank) and microgravity boiling reports (NTRS-20030003652).

In 0g, the lack of buoyancy keeps vapor bubbles from detaching quickly from heated surfaces, forming an insulating vapor barrier that drops thermal cooling efficiency to 68% compared to Earth (1g = 100%). Using a √g interpolation model across gravity regimes, our Suppression Sizing Module calculates:

  • Gravity-Bounded Cooling Efficiency (%) (68% in 0g, 80.8% on the Moon, 87.7% on Mars, 100% on Earth).
  • Estimated Flame Power (kW) derived from burn rate, sample geometry, and polymer heat of combustion (ΔHc).
  • Exact Water Mist Volume (mL) and % of the 2,720 mL ISS Extinguisher Tank required to quench the reaction heat (2,450 J/mL adjusted by cooling efficiency).
  • Estimated Discharge Time (seconds) needed to extinguish the fire—including operational alerts that confined electronics racks in 0g can take up to 60 seconds because fine mist cannot curve around obstacles without natural convection.

How It Works

  1. Mission & Habitat Configuration: Users select from mission presets (ISS Microgravity, Lunar Habitat, Martian Base, Earth Lab) or manually adjust gravity (g), oxygen concentration (% O2), cabin airflow (cm/s), and spacecraft material.
  2. Deterministic & PINN Evaluation: Clicking Simulate sends the parameters to our FastAPI backend, which checks for an exact BASS-II empirical match or runs our PINN + physics-bounded interpolation engine, returning the simulation state in under 5 ms.
  3. Interactive 3D Combustion Stage: The Unity WebGL chamber updates immediately, animating the flame's color, geometry, spread rate, and smoke/quench behavior in real time alongside our original MagicaVoxel spacecraft and extinguisher assets.
  4. Suppression Sizing & Telemetry Console: The console displays flame spread rate, LOI margin, CO/CO2 toxicity estimates, and the exact water mist volume (mL) and discharge time (seconds) required to extinguish the fire.
  5. Automated Engineering PDF Reports & BASS-II Explorer: Users can inspect the underlying 79 verified BASS-II experimental records and export a formatted engineering PDF report (@react-pdf/renderer) documenting the scenario, scientific boundaries, and suppression calculations.

Implementation Details

DATA PIPELINES & CUSTOM ML (backend/)

  • Datasets & Cleaning (backend/data/): Ingests and cleans BASS-II (PSI-25) experimental records into structured CSV/JSON baselines (bass2_empirical_verified.csv, bass2_empirical_verified.json) and stores trained model artifacts (pinn_model_weights.json, pinn_validation_metrics.json).
  • Custom PINN Pipeline (backend/app/ml_pipeline.py, backend/train_model.py): Pure-Python implementation of the Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network and Physics-Informed Classifier with Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation, trained and experimented in Google Colab with zero heavy ML runtime dependencies.
  • Physics & Suppression Engine (backend/app/physics_engine.py): Implements Olson, Bhattacharjee, and T'ien analytical bounds, √g cooling efficiency interpolation from UFSC/INPE VSB-30 and NASA NTRS data, and FWM PFE water volume and discharge time calculations.

BACKEND & API CONTRACT (backend/app/, contracts/, api/)

  • API Service (backend/app/main.py, api/index.py): FastAPI + Pydantic V2 service exposing deterministic simulation endpoints, investigation presets (investigations_presets.py), and automated tests (backend/tests/test_api.py).
  • Strict JSON Schema Contract (contracts/simulation_schema.json): Synchronizes backend outputs, frontend telemetry, and 3D simulator payloads.

3D SIMULATION & ASSETS (unity-fire-simulation/)

  • Engine & Shaders: Built in Unity (WebGL) with C# scripts and custom particle/flame shaders driven by backend telemetry.
  • Original Voxel Art: Custom 3D models (Earth, ISS, Moon, Mars, RocketShip, Extinguisher) modeled in MagicaVoxel (unity-fire-simulation/Assets/MagicaVoxelModels/).

FRONTEND (frontend/)

  • Stack: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Ajv (runtime JSON Schema validation against contracts/simulation_schema.json), @react-pdf/renderer (engineering PDF export), and Vitest + Testing Library for unit and route testing.

Impact

AstroFire 3D transforms fragmented microgravity combustion archives into a transparent, verifiable, and operationally useful engineering tool. By pairing a high-accuracy, physics-grounded neural network (94.94% accuracy, R² = 0.9117) with real-time 3D visualization, the platform makes the counterintuitive physics of space fires immediately visible to students, researchers, and mission designers.

Furthermore, by integrating Brazilian microgravity boiling research (UFSC/INPE VSB-30) with NASA's FWM PFE data, AstroFire 3D bridges the gap between theoretical combustion science and practical crew survival—quantifying the exact water mist volume and discharge time needed to suppress fires in 0g, lunar (0.16g), and Martian (0.38g) habitats.

Conclusion & Next Steps

AstroFire 3D demonstrates how deterministic physics, custom Physics-Informed Neural Networks, real-time 3D WebGL simulation, and international microgravity research can work together without relying on hallucination-prone black-box LLMs.

As our next technical milestones, we aim to:

  1. Expand the PINN dataset by integrating raw time-series and image data from SoFIE, Saffire IV–VI, and FLEX to cover thicker materials, depressurized atmospheres, and droplet suppression dynamics.
  2. Extend the 3D simulator from single-sample glovebox geometry to multi-material habitat rack layouts where ventilation wakes and obstacle shadowing affect flame spread and water mist reach.
  3. Collaborate with NASA combustion scientists and PSI maintainers to validate our PINN boundary assumptions and partial-gravity interpolation curves (0.16g and 0.38g) against upcoming lunar and Martian habitat standards.
